studies.title: Sestrin as a feedback inhibitor of TOR that prevents age-related pathologies
studies.authors: Lee JH; Budanov AV; Park EJ; Birse R; Kim TE; Perkins GA; Ocorr K; Ellisman MH; Bodmer R; Bier E; Karin M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: An early study linking Sestrin, later identified as a leucine sensor in mammals, to age-associated pathology in flies (fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, muscle and cardiac decline), prevented by TOR inhibition or AMPK activation. Sestrin sits in a negative feedback loop: TOR activity drives Sestrin expression, and Sestrin inhibits TOR back.

studies.title: Rapamycin improves healthspan but not inflammaging in nfκb1(-/-) mice.
studies.authors: Correia-Melo C; Birch J; Fielder E; Rahmatika D; Taylor J; Chapman J; Lagnado A; Carroll BM; Miwa S; Richardson G; Jurk D; Oakley F; Mann J; Mann DA; Korolchuk VI; Passos JF

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: nfkb1-knockout mice (genetically enhanced NF-kB activity, low-grade chronic inflammation, accelerated ageing); dietary rapamycin
studies.finding: Separates two effects of rapamycin that are usually assumed to travel together. In mice with genetically enhanced NF-kB activity, rapamycin showed no benefit in lifespan and no reduction of inflammaging, yet still reduced frailty and improved long-term memory, neuromuscular coordination and tissue architecture, with lower markers of cellular senescence. Healthspan benefit is therefore uncoupled here from suppression of inflammation, which is a boundary condition on the common claim that rapamycin acts on ageing mainly by damping inflammation. Note the mixed result: the healthspan outcomes are positive, the lifespan and inflammaging outcomes are null.

studies.title: Health Effects of Long-Term Rapamycin Treatment: The Impact on Mouse Health of Enteric Rapamycin Treatment from Four Months of Age throughout Life
studies.authors: Fischer KE; Gelfond JA; Soto VY; Han C; Someya S; Richardson A; Austad SN

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Male and female C57BL/6J mice fed microencapsulated rapamycin (14 ppm) or empty capsules from 4 months of age until death (40 per sex per group); repeated longitudinal health assessments from 16 months
studies.finding: Mice of both sexes were fed rapamycin in their food (14 ppm, encapsulated) from 4 months of age until death, 40 per sex per group, and the same animals were tested repeatedly for health measures from 16 months of age. Some measures improved: females had stronger grip at all ages, females kept body mass and fat longer during late-life weight loss, and sleep fragmentation fell in males (with a trend in females). Others did not change, such as stride length and age-related cochlear damage, and male rotarod performance was worse. In body mass, percent fat and resting metabolic rate, rapamycin moved males and females in opposite directions. The study showed that lifelong rapamycin in mice affects healthspan measures in a mixed and strongly sex-specific way rather than improving health across the board. Boundary: C57BL/6J mice only, one dietary dose; survival was reported in a companion paper, not in this one, and mTOR activity was not measured here.

studies.title: Rapamycin Attenuates Age-Related Changes in Marmoset Submandibular Gland: A Non-Human Primate Model of Human Oral Aging.
studies.authors: Abdul-Azees PA; Wang H; Chen J; Marinkovic M; Dean DD; Chen XD; Salmon AB; Yeh CK

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), chronic oral rapamycin, submandibular gland histology and immunofluorescence
studies.finding: In the aging marmoset submandibular gland the authors found fewer mucous and serous acinar units, expansion of ductal and collagen-rich stromal compartments, more extracellular matrix remodeling, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and more apoptotic and senescent cells. Chronic oral rapamycin was associated with partial preservation of acinar structure and with less fibrosis, lipid accumulation and fewer apoptotic and senescent cells, giving a tissue picture closer to that of younger animals. Boundary: histological and immunofluorescence associations in one tissue of a short-lived primate; the abstract gives no dose or group sizes, does not show that gland function improved, and reports no lifespan outcome.

relations.mechanism: Losing Drosophila Sestrin produces fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, muscle degeneration and cardiac malfunction, all prevented by inhibiting TOR or activating AMPK. Sestrin therefore limits age-associated pathology in the fly.
relations.mechanism_beginner: The only case in this atlas linking a nutrient sensor to ageing of a whole animal: fruit flies without this sensor build up fat and develop muscle and heart problems, and blocking this pathway or switching on AMPK prevents it. So the sensor holds age-related damage back. Watch what was measured – how sick the flies got, not how long they lived.
relations.boundary: Fly only, and the readout is age-related pathology: survival was never measured. No mammalian sensor-to-ageing evidence exists in this corpus.
relations.note: Added 2026-07-29. Gap H1 previously asserted the sensors link to ZERO ageing outcomes, which was true of the corpus but not of the literature.
